q.s: A newborn has severe respiratory distress immediately after birth. His abdomen is scaphoid, bowel sounds are heard in the left chest, and the heart sounds are best heard on the right. Chest x-ray shows bowel loops in the left hemithorax.
o: Pulmonary hypoplasia from compression of the developing lung
cl: bowel sounds are heard in the left chest
heart sounds are best heard on the right
q.ch: Left congenital diaphragmatic hernia → bowel compresses the developing lung → pulmonary hypoplasia.
q.tr: Bilateral renal agenesis (Potter sequence) also causes pulmonary hypoplasia.
q.q2: What is the main cause of his poor gas exchange?

q.s: A 30-year-old woman has an incidental finding on chest x-ray: a round, sharply defined, fluid-density mass in the middle mediastinum near the carina. She has had two episodes of pneumonia in the right lower lobe.
q.ch: Smooth fluid-filled middle mediastinal mass + recurrent infection → bronchogenic cyst → abnormal foregut budding.
q.tr: The cyst may appear air-filled if infected.
q.q2: What is the embryologic origin of this lesion?

q.s: A researcher studies cells in the bronchioles that are nonciliated, cuboidal and contain secretory granules. These cells contain high levels of cytochrome P-450 and regenerate the bronchiolar lining after injury.
q.ch: Bronchiolar secretory cell + P-450 + stem cell function → club cell.
q.tr: Type II pneumocytes regenerate the alveolar lining.
q.q2: Which cells are being studied?
q.fc: Regional ventilation and blood flow in the upright lung

q.s: A 45-year-old man with reactivated tuberculosis has a cavitary lesion at the lung apex. His physician explains why TB prefers this region using the regional distribution of ventilation and blood flow shown.
o: About 0.6; low oxygen tension favors TB
Infinity; no blood flow favors TB
About 0.6; high blood flow brings more macrophages
About 2–3; high V/Q gives high PO2 that TB thrives in
cl: cavitary lesion at the lung apex
regional distribution of ventilation and blood flow
q.ch: At apex ventilation 45 / flow 20 ≈ 2–3 → high V/Q → high alveolar PO2 → aerobic TB thrives.
q.tr: Both ventilation and perfusion are greater at the base.
q.q2: What is the approximate V/Q ratio at the apex, and why does TB favor it?

q.s: A 40-year-old man has a tidal volume of 600 mL, respiratory rate of 15/min, arterial PCO2 of 40 mm Hg and mixed expired PCO2 of 28 mm Hg.
cl: mixed expired PCO2 of 28 mm Hg
q.ch: Bohr: VD = VT × (PaCO2 − PECO2)/PaCO2 = 180 mL → VA = (VT − VD) × RR = 6.3 L/min.
q.tr: Rapid shallow breathing wastes a larger fraction on dead space.
q.q2: What is his alveolar ventilation?
q.fc: Static pressure–volume curves of the lungs from three patients

q.s: A 67-year-old former smoker has progressive dyspnea, a dry cough and fine bibasilar velcro-like crackles. He has digital clubbing. CT shows peripheral reticular opacities with honeycombing at the bases. Pressure–volume curves from three patients are shown.
q.ch: IPF → stiff lungs → low compliance (flat curve C) → antifibrotics slow decline.
q.tr: Emphysema has high compliance (steep curve A).
q.q2: Which curve matches this patient, and which treatment can slow his disease?

q.s: A 35-year-old woman has worsening shortness of breath, double vision at the end of the day and difficulty chewing. Her chest x-ray and CT show normal lung parenchyma. Her pulmonary function tests are shown.
o: Respiratory muscle weakness from myasthenia gravis
cl: double vision at the end of the day
q.ch: Restrictive pattern (low TLC, normal ratio) + normal DLCO and A-a gradient + myasthenia → respiratory muscle weakness.
q.tr: Interstitial disease lowers DLCO and raises the A-a gradient.
q.q2: Which best explains this PFT pattern?
q.fc: Oxygen equilibration along the pulmonary capillary. Dotted line = alveolar PO2 (100 mm Hg).

q.s: A 55-year-old woman with systemic sclerosis has dyspnea that worsens with exercise. Her oxygen saturation is normal at rest but falls with walking. Capillary PO2 measurements from a study are shown.
o: Oxygen transfer is diffusion limited because the alveolar wall is thickened
The pattern shows a right-to-left shunt
Oxygen transfer is limited by decreased alveolar PO2
The pattern shows carbon monoxide poisoning
Her CO2 transfer will fail first
cl: Shorter capillary transit time with exercise.
q.ch: Thickened alveolar wall (↑ Δx in Fick's law) → O2 does not equilibrate by capillary end → diffusion limited → exercise hypoxemia.
q.tr: Fibrosis causes hypoxemia before hypercapnia.
q.q2: Which statement best describes oxygen transfer in her lungs?

q.s: A 30-year-old man with a large ventricular septal defect has developed cyanosis and clubbing. His arterial PO2 is 52 mm Hg on room air. After 15 minutes of 100% oxygen, his PaO2 is 58 mm Hg.
cl: After 15 minutes of 100% oxygen, his PaO2 is 58 mm Hg
q.ch: Shunted blood bypasses alveoli → 100% O2 cannot oxygenate it → hypoxemia persists.
q.tr: In V/Q mismatch, 100% O2 does improve PaO2.
q.q2: What best explains the poor response to oxygen?

q.s: A man with chronic bronchitis lives at sea level. His lung bases are poorly ventilated because of mucus plugging. Over years he develops a loud P2 and right ventricular hypertrophy.
o: Hypoxic vasoconstriction diverting blood to well-ventilated regions
cl: poorly ventilated because of mucus plugging
q.ch: Low PAO2 → hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction → chronic ↑ PVR → pulmonary hypertension → RVH.
q.tr: Systemic vessels dilate in response to hypoxia.
q.q2: Which local response in the pulmonary arterioles led to these findings?

q.s: A 28-year-old woman with heavy menstrual bleeding has a hemoglobin of 7.5 g/dL. Her PaO2 is 98 mm Hg and SaO2 is 99%. She has fatigue and exercise intolerance.
q.ch: O2 content = 1.34 × Hb × SaO2 + 0.003 × PaO2 → halved Hb → halved content, normal PaO2 and SaO2.
q.tr: CO poisoning lowers SaO2 and content with a normal PaO2.
q.q2: Which is reduced in her blood?

q.s: A pregnant woman asks how oxygen crosses the placenta to her baby even though fetal blood has a lower PO2 than her own.
o: It binds 2,3-BPG less, giving higher oxygen affinity
It is a monomer like myoglobin
Its curve is shifted to the right
cl: fetal blood has a lower PO2
crosses the placenta to her baby
q.ch: HbF binds 2,3-BPG poorly → higher O2 affinity (left shift) → pulls O2 from maternal Hb.
q.tr: Left shift = lower P50.
q.q2: Which property of fetal hemoglobin explains this?

q.s: A 55-year-old man has had a productive cough every winter for the past 4 years, lasting about 4 months each time. He has smoked a pack a day for 35 years. He has rhonchi and mild cyanosis. Hematocrit is 55%.
o: Destruction of alveolar walls distal to terminal bronchioles
Permanently dilated bronchi with purulent debris
Mucus gland hyperplasia with a Reid index above 50%
cl: productive cough every winter for the past 4 years
q.ch: Chronic productive cough in a smoker → chronic bronchitis → mucous gland hyperplasia (Reid index > 50%).
q.tr: Squamous metaplasia of the bronchial epithelium also occurs.
q.q2: Which histologic finding is expected in his bronchi?
q.fc: Family pedigree. The parents (I-1 and I-2) are first cousins.

q.s: A 25-year-old woman has had chronic sinusitis, recurrent ear infections and a productive cough since childhood. She and her husband have been unable to conceive. Chest x-ray shows the heart on the right side, and CT shows bronchiectasis. Her family history is shown.
o: Dynein arm defect causing immotile cilia
cl: Immotile sperm or ciliary defect in tubes.
q.ch: Sinusitis + bronchiectasis + infertility + situs inversus + autosomal recessive pedigree → dynein defect.
q.tr: Cystic fibrosis is the most common cause of bronchiectasis.
q.q2: What is the underlying defect?

q.s: A 38-year-old woman with long-standing asthma has worsening wheeze and coughs up brown mucus plugs. Her eosinophils are 1200/μL and total IgE is very high. CT shows central bronchiectasis with mucus impaction.
q.ch: Asthma + eosinophilia + high IgE + central bronchiectasis → ABPA → Aspergillus.
q.tr: ABPA also complicates cystic fibrosis.
q.q2: Which organism is driving this condition?

q.s: A 52-year-old engineer who has worked in aerospace manufacturing for 20 years has progressive dyspnea. CT shows upper-lobe nodules and hilar lymphadenopathy. Biopsy shows noncaseating granulomas. Lymphocyte proliferation testing to a workplace metal is positive.
q.ch: Beryllium exposure → cell-mediated granulomas → steroid-responsive berylliosis.
q.tr: Berylliosis mimics sarcoidosis.
q.q2: Which treatment may improve his lung disease?

q.s: A 60-year-old retired coal miner with rheumatoid arthritis has multiple 1–5 cm nodules scattered through both lungs on chest x-ray. He has no fever or weight loss.
q.ch: Pneumoconiosis + rheumatoid arthritis + intrapulmonary nodules → Caplan syndrome.
q.tr: Caplan syndrome also occurs with silicosis and asbestosis.
q.q2: What is the most likely diagnosis?

q.s: A 74-year-old man who installed insulation for 30 years has right chest pain and weight loss. CT shows thick, nodular pleura encasing the right lung and a bloody effusion. Biopsy cells are positive for calretinin and cytokeratin 5/6.
o: It stains positive for CEA like carcinomas
Smoking is not a risk factor
It is usually cured with surgery
It typically arises in the upper lobe apex
cl: thick, nodular pleura encasing the right lung
q.ch: Asbestos exposure + pleural rind + hemorrhagic effusion + calretinin positive → mesothelioma.
q.tr: EM shows long microvilli; psammoma bodies may be present.
q.q2: Which statement about this tumor is correct?

q.s: A 70-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy and an ejection fraction of 20% has disturbed sleep. His wife notices that his breathing gradually gets deeper and faster, then slows and stops for 20 seconds, in repeated cycles. There is no snoring.
o: Central sleep apnea with Cheyne-Stokes respiration
e: Wrong. Effort against blocked airway, snoring.
cl: gradually gets deeper and faster, then slows and stops
q.ch: Heart failure → delayed chemoreceptor feedback → central apnea with Cheyne-Stokes cycles.
q.tr: Opioids and CNS injury also cause central sleep apnea.
q.q2: What type of sleep-disordered breathing is this?

q.s: A 7-year-old boy snores loudly every night, breathes through his mouth and has pauses in breathing during sleep. His teacher says he is inattentive. He has a normal weight.
q.ch: Child with snoring + apneas → obstructive sleep apnea → adenotonsillar hypertrophy.
q.tr: In adults, excess parapharyngeal tissue (obesity) is the usual cause.
q.q2: What is the most likely cause?

q.s: A 28-year-old man is stabbed in the left chest. He is short of breath with a BP of 78/44 mm Hg, heart rate of 134/min and distended neck veins. Breath sounds are absent on the left and the trachea is shifted to the right.
o: Needle decompression followed by chest tube
e: Wrong. Tamponade has normal breath sounds.
cl: Breath sounds are absent on the left
trachea is shifted to the right
q.ch: Penetrating trauma + hypotension + JVD + absent breath sounds + tracheal shift away → tension pneumothorax → decompress.
q.tr: Mediastinal shift kinks the IVC, reducing venous return.
q.q2: What is the immediate next step?

q.s: A 60-year-old woman has dyspnea 2 days after abdominal surgery. Her right lower chest is dull to percussion with decreased breath sounds and decreased fremitus. The trachea is pulled toward the right. Chest x-ray shows a collapsed right lower lobe.
o: Obstruction of a bronchus by a mucus plug
cl: The trachea is pulled toward the right
q.ch: Postoperative mucus plug → air resorbed distally → obstructive atelectasis → trachea shifts toward lesion.
q.tr: Incentive spirometry helps prevent it.
q.q2: Which mechanism of atelectasis is most likely?

q.s: A 72-year-old man with an ejection fraction of 25% has worsening orthopnea and bilateral leg edema. He has bilateral pleural effusions, larger on the right. A diagnostic thoracentesis is done. The results are shown.
o: Decreased oncotic pressure from nephrotic syndrome
q.ch: Protein ratio 0.28, LDH ratio 0.4 → transudate → heart failure → ↑ hydrostatic pressure.
q.tr: Transudates usually do not need drainage.
q.q2: What mechanism produced this effusion?

q.s: A 70-year-old man died 6 days after the onset of lobar pneumonia from Streptococcus pneumoniae. At autopsy, the affected lobe is uniformly gray and firm. Microscopy shows alveoli packed with neutrophils, lysed red cells and fibrin.
q.ch: Day 6 + gray lobe + WBCs, lysed RBCs and fibrin → gray hepatization.
q.tr: In resolution, macrophages digest the exudate.
q.q2: Which stage of lobar pneumonia is this?

q.s: A 20-year-old college student has had 2 weeks of a dry, hacking cough, low-grade fever, headache and fatigue, but is still attending classes. Chest x-ray shows patchy bilateral interstitial infiltrates that look worse than he appears. Cold agglutinins are positive.
q.ch: Young adult + walking pneumonia + interstitial infiltrates + cold agglutinins → Mycoplasma.
q.tr: Interstitial pneumonia localizes to the alveolar walls.
q.q2: Which organism is most likely?

q.s: A 58-year-old woman has had cough, fever and malaise for 6 weeks. Three courses of antibiotics have not helped. Sputum and blood cultures are negative. CT shows patchy consolidations, and biopsy shows plugs of granulation tissue in bronchioles and alveolar ducts.
cl: Three courses of antibiotics have not helped
plugs of granulation tissue in bronchioles
q.ch: Antibiotic-resistant pneumonia + negative cultures + bronchiolar granulation plugs → COP → steroids.
q.tr: COP was formerly called BOOP.
q.q2: What is the most appropriate treatment?

q.s: A 45-year-old woman under general anesthesia vomits and aspirates gastric contents. Two hours later she is tachypneic with wheezing and hypoxemia. Chest x-ray shows new infiltrates in both lower lobes. She has no fever.
q.ch: Gastric acid aspiration → chemical pneumonitis within hours → supportive care.
q.tr: Aspiration pneumonia develops days later from infection.
q.q2: What is the mechanism of her lung injury?

q.s: A 24-year-old man fractured both femurs in a motorcycle crash. Thirty-six hours later he becomes confused and short of breath. He has petechiae on his chest, axillae and conjunctivae.
cl: petechiae on his chest, axillae and conjunctivae
q.ch: Long bone fracture + hypoxemia + confusion + petechiae → fat embolism syndrome.
q.tr: Liposuction can also cause fat emboli.
q.q2: What is the most likely diagnosis?

q.s: A 35-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis has a mass in the anterior mediastinum on CT.
q.ch: Myasthenia gravis + anterior mediastinal mass → thymoma.
q.tr: Anterior masses: thyroid, thymoma, teratoma, "terrible" lymphoma.
q.q2: Which mass is most likely?

q.s: A 42-year-old man has severe chest pain after repeated forceful vomiting during a night of heavy drinking. There is crepitus over his neck. A crunching sound is heard with each heartbeat.
cl: crunching sound is heard with each heartbeat
q.ch: Forceful vomiting → transmural esophageal rupture → pneumomediastinum (Hamman sign).
q.tr: Mallory-Weiss tears are mucosal and do not leak air.
q.q2: What is the source of the air in his mediastinum?

head: Finding
Result
rows: 2.5-cm well-circumscribed endobronchial mass, left main bronchus
Nests of uniform cells with salt-and-pepper chromatin

q.s: A 38-year-old woman who has never smoked has episodes of wheezing in her left chest, facial flushing and diarrhea. Her findings are shown.
o: It always transforms into small cell carcinoma
Poor; it is unresponsive to surgery
Very poor; most patients die within 1 year
Intermediate; it often spreads to the pleura
q.ch: Endobronchial mass + neuroendocrine nests + 5-HIAA + flushing → bronchial carcinoid → excellent prognosis.
q.tr: Small cell carcinoma is also neuroendocrine but highly aggressive.
q.q2: What is the expected prognosis of this tumor?

q.s: A 66-year-old man with a 60-pack-year history has a large peripheral lung mass. Biopsy shows sheets of pleomorphic giant cells without glands or keratin. He has developed breast enlargement.
q.ch: Peripheral anaplastic giant-cell tumor + gynecomastia → large cell carcinoma producing hCG.
q.tr: Large cell carcinoma is treated surgically and has a poor prognosis.
q.q2: Which hormone explains his breast enlargement?

q.s: A 76-year-old man takes an over-the-counter sleep aid containing diphenhydramine. Two days later he is confused, constipated, has a dry mouth and cannot urinate. He has an enlarged prostate.
cl: confused, constipated, has a dry mouth
q.ch: First-generation H1-blockers cross the BBB and block muscarinic receptors → confusion, retention.
q.tr: Second-generation agents (loratadine) cause less sedation.
q.q2: Which property of the drug caused these effects?

q.s: A 30-year-old woman taking fluoxetine drinks a whole bottle of cough syrup for a cold. She develops agitation, tremor, sweating, a temperature of 39.4 °C and inducible clonus.
q.ch: Dextromethorphan + SSRI → serotonin syndrome (agitation, hyperthermia, clonus).
q.tr: At high doses dextromethorphan also causes dissociative NMDA effects.
q.q2: Which ingredient most likely caused this reaction?

q.s: A 70-year-old man with COPD takes theophylline. He is started on ciprofloxacin for pneumonia. Three days later he has nausea, palpitations and a seizure.
o: Ciprofloxacin directly causes seizures by GABA agonism
Theophylline has a wide therapeutic index
Ciprofloxacin inhibits cytochrome P-450, raising theophylline levels
q.ch: Ciprofloxacin inhibits CYP1A2 → ↑ theophylline → arrhythmias and seizures.
q.tr: Theophylline inhibits PDE and blocks adenosine.
q.q2: What explains his toxicity?

q.s: A 60-year-old man with pulmonary arterial hypertension takes sildenafil. He develops chest pain at home and takes a sublingual nitroglycerin tablet. Minutes later he faints with a blood pressure of 70/40 mm Hg.
o: Nitrates raise cGMP production while sildenafil blocks its breakdown
Sildenafil inhibits nitrate metabolism in the liver
cl: faints with a blood pressure of 70/40 mm Hg
q.ch: Nitrate → NO → ↑ cGMP; PDE-5 inhibitor prevents cGMP breakdown → profound vasodilation → hypotension.
q.tr: PDE-5 inhibitors are contraindicated with nitrates.
q.q2: What is the mechanism of this interaction?

q.s: A 50-year-old woman with severe pulmonary arterial hypertension is started on a continuous IV infusion through a central line. She develops flushing, jaw pain and headache.
o: Prostacyclin analog that vasodilates and inhibits platelet aggregation
cl: continuous IV infusion through a central line
q.ch: Prostacyclin (PGI2) analog → ↑ cAMP → pulmonary and systemic vasodilation → flushing, jaw pain.
q.tr: Iloprost is an inhaled prostacyclin analog.
q.q2: What is the mechanism of this drug?

q.s: A 52-year-old woman with allergic asthma has frequent attacks despite high-dose inhaled glucocorticoids and a long-acting β2-agonist. Her serum IgE is markedly elevated, and skin testing is positive for dust mites.
o: Omalizumab; it binds free IgE and blocks binding to FcεRI
cl: high-dose inhaled glucocorticoids and a long-acting β2-agonist
q.ch: Severe allergic asthma with high IgE → omalizumab → less IgE on mast cells → fewer attacks.
q.tr: Omalizumab is also used for chronic urticaria and nasal polyps.
q.q2: Which drug is most appropriate to add, and how does it work?

q.s: A 45-year-old man has used an over-the-counter decongestant nasal spray several times a day for 3 weeks. His nasal congestion is now worse whenever he stops using it. His blood pressure is 152/94 mm Hg.
cl: several times a day for 3 weeks
worse whenever he stops using it
q.ch: α-agonist decongestant → vasoconstriction; prolonged use → tachyphylaxis and rebound congestion.
q.tr: Limit use to 4–6 days.
q.q2: What is the mechanism of the decongestant?

q.s: A 55-year-old woman has a fever and severe left facial pain over her cheek for 10 days after a cold. Now her left eyelid is swollen and red, and she has pain with eye movements and double vision.
o: The sphenoid sinus via the optic canal
The frontal sinus via the cribriform plate
The thin orbital floor and medial wall from the maxillary and ethmoid sinuses
e: Wrong. Not the primary sinus here.
cl: severe left facial pain over her cheek
pain with eye movements and double vision
q.ch: Maxillary/ethmoid sinusitis → spread through thin orbital walls → orbital cellulitis.
q.tr: Infection can also reach the cavernous sinus and meninges.
q.q2: Through which structure did the infection most likely spread to the orbit?
